summary: Jacob reaches Goshen and joyfully reunites with Joseph, who supplies the family through the famine while acquiring Egypt's land, people, and cattle for Pharaoh in exchange for food. After the river's flooding restores agriculture, Joseph establishes a one-fifth levy; Jacob later dies, is buried in Canaan, and entrusts the ancestral books to Levi.
whyItMatters: The chapter completes Jacob's reunion and burial promises while showing the wider political cost of famine administration. Its final transfer of books to Levi makes preservation of ancestral instruction part of the family's legacy.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: Goshen and Egypt during famine and agricultural recovery, followed by Jacob's burial in the ancestral cave near Hebron.
context.literaryForm: Reunion narrative, economic-administrative summary, patriarchal death notice, and transmission of books.

before.text: God has assured Jacob that he may enter Egypt and will be returned for burial; the household has been directed toward Goshen.

here.text: Distinguish the family's generous provision from the larger Egyptian transfer of land and people to Pharaoh, then follow Jacob's final blessings and burial.

after.text: After Jacob dies, the family grows during Joseph's life, but the death of that generation and conflict among rulers lead toward enslavement.

outline.heading: Reunion and family joy
outline.note: Jacob embraces the living Joseph and sees the brothers eating together.

outline.heading: Settlement and famine provision
outline.note: Joseph gives his family a place to live and food while Egypt’s resources pass to Pharaoh.

outline.heading: Flood, sowing, and the fifth
outline.note: The river’s renewed flooding enables recovery and a continuing royal levy.

outline.heading: Jacob’s final legacy
outline.note: His death, blessings, burial, and transfer of books to Levi close his story.

keyVerses.text: And Joseph and his brothers eat bread before their father and drank wine, and Jacob rejoiced with exceeding great joy because he saw Joseph eating with his brothers and drinking before him, and he blessed the Creator of all things who had preserved him, and had preserved for him his twelve sons.
keyVerses.why: Jacob’s joy centers on seeing Joseph alive and at table with his brothers.

keyVerses.text: And the land of Egypt suffered by reason of the famine, and Joseph acquired all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh in return for food, and he got possession of the people and their cattle and everything for Pharaoh.
keyVerses.why: The acquisition of land, people, and cattle for Pharaoh reveals the coercive consequences of scarcity.

keyVerses.text: And he gave all his books and the books of his fathers to Levi his son that he might preserve them and renew them for his children until this day.
keyVerses.why: The final verse assigns Levi custody and renewal of Jacob’s and his fathers’ books.

questions.question: Why does seeing the brothers eat together matter to Jacob?
questions.answer: He can see both that Joseph is alive and that the sons share a meal in his presence. The narrator describes this as the preservation of his twelve sons and a reason for blessing the creator.

questions.question: What is the family given in Egypt?
questions.answer: Joseph grants a right to dwell in Goshen, Rameses, and the surrounding region under his authority. He also supplies sufficient bread to sustain his father, brothers, and their holdings through the famine.

questions.question: Does famine relief benefit all Egyptians on the same terms as Joseph’s family?
questions.answer: The chapter says Joseph acquires their land, people, cattle, and everything for Pharaoh in return for food. That transfer under conditions of hunger is a profound loss of autonomy and property, even though the narrative also credits him with keeping people supplied.

questions.question: What changes when the famine ends?
questions.answer: The river again overflows the land, whereas during the famine it had watered only limited areas near its banks. Joseph supplies seed and food, and the renewed sowing produces an abundant harvest.

questions.question: What is the “fifth part”?
questions.answer: It is one portion out of five of the harvest taken for Pharaoh, with four portions left for food and seed. The narrator describes that share as an ordinance continuing to the account's own present.

questions.question: How do the death notices relate to the earlier promise?
questions.answer: Jacob lives seventeen years in Egypt, blesses his sons, and is buried in the ancestral cave in Canaan. The burial completes the return to the land promised in the departure scene without requiring Jacob to have moved home while alive.

questions.question: Why are the books given to Levi?
questions.answer: The text explicitly assigns him the task of preserving and renewing both Jacob's books and the books of the earlier ancestors for his children. It identifies custodianship and transmission, without supplying a catalogue of all the books involved.

glossary.def: One-fifth of the harvest, established as Pharaoh’s share while the rest supplies food and seed.
A standing regulation, used here for the royal share of agricultural produce.
The ancestral burial place in Canaan where Jacob is laid after dying in Egypt.
